THE ARGUED LORD AND THE UNEXPLAINABLE IGNORANCE: THE IPVV AGAINST ADVAITA VEDĀNTA

The anti-anirvācya argument, the difference that is real, and the two nondualisms compared

  • magnum-opus essay. 2026-08-11. Advaita Vedānta and the Pratyabhijñā are the two great nondualisms
  • India — both hold that reality is nondual consciousness. But they are profoundly opposed. Advaita
  • sits an un-explainable ignorance (anirvācyā avidyā) to account for the appearance of plurality;
  • e Pratyabhijñā (in the IPVV) rejects this, arguing that the difference is real — the self's own
  • flection, not the product of an un-explainable ignorance. This essay is the complete comparative
  • nthesis of the two. It expounds the IPVV's anti-anirvācya argument in full (V3I, the kāryakāraṇatā
  • marśa), contrasts the two accounts of plurality and liberation, and shows that the two nondualisms
  • verge at the point where the Pratyabhijñā makes consciousness free (and the world real) and Advaita
  • kes it passive (and the world illusory). The comparison is grounded in the IPVV's L2 layer and the
  • shing-tantraloka sessions, and it is now possible in full because the IPVV is translated.*

PART I — THE TWO NONDUALISMS

1.1 Advaita Vedānta

  • vaita Vedānta, systematized by Śaṅkara (c. 8th century), holds that reality is one nondual
  • nsciousness — Brahman — and that the plurality of the world is an appearance produced by ignorance
  • vidyā). The individual self (jīva) and the world are superimpositions (adhyāsa) on Brahman, caused by
  • ignorance that is itself "un-explainable" (anirvācya) — neither real (for it produces the appearance
  • plurality) nor unreal (for it appears), neither existent nor non-existent.
  • e structure of Advaita:
  • `
  • ahman (pure nondual consciousness)
  • avidyā (anirvācya, the un-explainable ignorance)
  • the apparent individual (jīva) and world
  • `
  • beration is the removal of the ignorance — the realization that the jīva is Brahman. It is
  • nowledge* that liberates: the knowledge that removes the avidyā that superimposed the plurality.

1.2 The Pratyabhijñā (the recognition school)

  • e Pratyabhijñā, founded by Utpaladeva and systematized by Abhinavagupta, also holds that reality is
  • e nondual consciousness — but it is a free consciousness, Śiva, and the world is a real
  • nifestation, not an appearance produced by ignorance.
  • e structure of the Pratyabhijñā:
  • `
  • va (one free, self-aware consciousness)
  • svātantrya (freedom) + māyāśakti (the power of manifestation)
  • the real world as the self's own reflection
  • `
  • beration is recognition — the re-cognition of the self as the Lord. It is recognition that
  • berates: the re-cognition that removes the false identification (not an ignorance-produced
  • perimposition but a misreading of the self's real manifestation).

1.3 The question of the comparison

  • e two nondualisms agree that reality is nondual consciousness. They differ on three things:
  • The nature of consciousness: passive (Advaita) or free (Pratyabhijñā)?
  • The status of the world: illusory appearance (Advaita) or real manifestation (Pratyabhijñā)?
  • The cause of plurality: un-explainable ignorance (Advaita) or the self's own freedom
  • ratyabhijñā)?
  • The thesis of this essay.** The comparison turns on the third difference, and it is there that the
  • VV makes its decisive argument. The IPVV rejects the Advaitin's anirvācya (the un-explainable
  • norance) — not merely by asserting its alternative but by arguing that the un-explainable ignorance
  • incoherent. The argument (V3I): if the difference of the world is the product of an un-explainable
  • norance, then of whom is this ignorance? The one-form Brahman cannot have it; the separate souls
  • uld be raised up by it; and "un-explainable" is the speech of a yakṣa — a being we cannot pin down.
  • e IPVV's alternative: the difference is real, the self's own reflection — and the bondage is the
  • isreading* of that real difference as external separation.

PART II — THE ANTI-ANIRVĀCYA ARGUMENT (V3I)

2.1 The argument, in full

  • e IPVV's anti-anirvācya argument is in the kāryakāraṇatā vimarśa (V3I), the close of the analysis of
  • usality. The context: the IPVV has argued that causality is the conscious knower's agency, and that
  • e difference of things is real, not mere ignorance. The Advaitin objects: if all is one consciousness,
  • en the difference must be ignorance — an un-explainable (anirvācya) illusion.
  • e IPVV's reply is a systematic demolition:
"If consciousness is one, and the difference is ignorance, then we must ask: of whom is this
ignorance? The one-form Brahman cannot have an ignorance that is the mere absence of something else.
Nor can the separate souls exist — they too would be raised up by the ignorance. If the ignorance is
called 'un-explainable' (anirvācya), then we still do not know whose it is; 'it shines and yet is
un-explainable' is the speech of a yakṣa, a being we cannot pin down." (V3I)
  • e argument has four steps:
  • The one-form Brahman cannot have the ignorance. If reality is one, nondual, pure consciousness,
  • en an ignorance is "the mere absence of something else" — but there is no "something else" in a
  • ndual reality for the ignorance to be the absence of. The one-form Brahman cannot have an
  • norance that presupposes a duality to be absent from.
  • The separate souls cannot ground it either. If the ignorance is to belong to the separate souls
  • he jīvas), then the souls must exist as separate — but they are supposed to be produced by the
  • norance. The souls would be raised up by the very ignorance they are supposed to bear. This is a
  • cious circle: the ignorance produces the souls, but the souls are the ones who have the ignorance.
  • "Un-explainable" does not help. Calling the ignorance anirvācya (neither real nor unreal, neither
  • istent nor non-existent) does not tell us whose it is. "It shines and yet is un-explainable" is
  • e speech of a yakṣa — a being we cannot pin down, a mystery that explains nothing. The anirvācya is
  • t an explanation; it is a refusal to explain, dressed as a technical term.
  • The refutation is self-undermining. If the difference of the world is ignorance, then the very
  • efutation" that would remove the difference is itself a manifestation — and so would be a
  • fference, and so would be ignorance. The attempt to dismiss the world as an un-explainable illusion
  • uts the horns of the hare's head and plucks the sky-flower." Even the revealed teaching, if it
  • aches the world is illusion, would itself be ignorance — a net of illusions.

2.2 The force of the argument

  • e anti-anirvācya argument is a genuine refutation, not a mere assertion of the alternative. It shows
  • at the Advaitin's account of plurality is internally incoherent:
  • The ignorance cannot belong to Brahman (nondual, hence no "something else" for it to be the absence
  • ).
  • It cannot belong to the souls (they are produced by it, so they cannot bear it).
  • "Un-explainable" is a refusal to answer, not an answer.
  • The refutation self-undermines (it is itself a manifestation, hence a difference, hence an
  • norance).
  • e upshot: the Advaitin's plurality requires an ignorance that cannot be located anywhere. The
  • atyabhijñā's alternative — the difference is real, the self's own manifestation — is not only more
  • sitive; it is the only coherent account, because it locates the plurality in the freedom of
  • nsciousness rather than in a mysterious ignorance.

2.3 The "not absolute monism" clause

  • e IPVV adds a crucial clause:
"And indeed, 'even Brahman with ignorance is [admitted by some], so this is not an absolute monism
either.'" (V3I)
  • is is a subtle and important qualification. The IPVV acknowledges that even the Advaitin's Brahman is
  • t absolute monism in the strict sense — it admits an ignorance, a second principle that produces
  • urality. So neither is the Pratyabhijñā a bare monism that denies difference; the difference is real.
  • e system is a "qualified" nondualism: one reality, really manifesting as the many through its freedom.

PART III — THE DIFFERENCE THAT IS REAL

3.1 The difference is real: the self's own reflection

  • e IPVV's positive account of the difference is the pratibimbavāda — the reflection-model. The
  • fference of the world is real because it is the self's own reflection, not a superimposition over
  • thing.
  • e pushing-tantraloka session on the difference (difference-real-at-śiva) drew out the TĀ's parallel:
"The Buddhist... serves to illustrate that the world is just an unreal appearance. It appears, but
has no independent nature of its own, like a reflection in a mirror. However, Abhinava, following the
lead of Utpaladeva, takes care to stress that the reflections are real. The face reflected in the
mirror is my own. It is a true reflection, not a mistake." (TĀ, the pratibimbavāda)
  • The point.** The world's difference is not an unreal appearance to be dismissed; it is the self's
  • n reflection — "my own face" in the mirror of consciousness. This is the direct answer to Advaita:
  • ere Advaita says the world is an unreal appearance (a superimposition), the Pratyabhijñā says it is a
  • eal* reflection (the self's own manifestation).

3.2 The two senses of "difference"

  • e comparison requires a precise distinction between two senses of "difference" — and this is the key
  • reconciling the Pratyabhijñā's own claims:
  • Difference as real manifestation (the pratibimbavāda): the difference of things is real because
  • is the self's own reflection — the world is the self's manifestation. This is what the IPVV and
  • e TĀ affirm: the reflections are real.
  • Difference as separation (māyīya, the impurity): the false reading that the difference
  • dicates independent external substances — the ego's externalization, the exhaustiveness-claim.
  • is is what the master-key's impurities session called the contracted power.
  • The distinction, applied.** The real difference = the self's reflection; the impurity = the
  • isreading* of that real difference as external separation. Recognition does not remove the difference
  • t is real); it removes the misreading (the externality). Nothing added, nothing removed — the
  • fference is real, and the bondage is its misreading.
  • is is the Pratyabhijñā's answer to Advaita's account of plurality: the plurality is real (the self's
  • flection), and the bondage is not the plurality but the misreading of it. Advaita needs an
  • norance to produce an illusory plurality; the Pratyabhijñā needs no ignorance — it needs only the
  • eedom of consciousness to manifest really, and the misreading that takes the manifestation as external.

3.3 The freedom vs. the passivity

  • e deepest divergence between the two nondualisms is the nature of consciousness:
  • Advaita's Brahman is passive.* Brahman is pure consciousness, but it does not *act — it does not
  • nifest the world; the world is superimposed by an ignorance that is not Brahman's doing. Brahman is
  • e witness, not the agent.
  • The Pratyabhijñā's Śiva is free.* Śiva is not only self-aware but *free (svātantrya) — he manifests
  • e world by his own will, as his own self-expression. The world is not superimposed by an ignorance; it
  • created by the freedom of consciousness.
  • The consequence for plurality.** Because Advaita's Brahman is passive, the plurality must come from
  • tside — hence the ignorance. Because the Pratyabhijñā's Śiva is free, the plurality comes from within
  • hence the real manifestation. The divergence on the nature of consciousness (passive vs. free)
  • ntails* the divergence on plurality (ignorance vs. manifestation). The IPVV's anti-anirvācya argument
  • the negative face of this; the pratibimbavāda is the positive face.

PART IV — LIBERATION COMPARED

4.1 Advaita's liberation: knowledge that removes the ignorance

  • vaita's liberation is knowledge — the realization that the jīva is Brahman, which removes the
  • norance that superimposed the plurality. It is a removal of a false superimposition, by knowledge.

4.2 The Pratyabhijñā's liberation: recognition of the self

  • e Pratyabhijñā's liberation is recognition — the re-cognition of the self as the Lord, which removes
  • e false identification (not an ignorance-produced superimposition but a misreading of the real
  • nifestation). It is a removal of a false self-positioning, by recognition.

4.3 The comparison

  • e two liberations are structurally similar (both remove a false appearance by a transformative
  • gnition) but differ on what is removed:
  • Advaita removes the ignorance-produced plurality. The world, the jīva, the plurality are
  • pearances; liberation removes the ignorance and the appearances with it. The world is left behind.
  • The Pratyabhijñā removes the misreading of the real plurality. The world is real (the self's
  • flection); liberation removes the misreading of it as external. The world is not left behind; it
  • recognized as the self's own reflection — "the face in the mirror is my own."
  • The jīvanmukta vs. the videhamukta.** The Pratyabhijñā's jīvanmukta (the one liberated while living)
  • ves in the world, free — because the world is real and the recognition re-cognizes it. Advaita's
  • beration, by contrast, is the removal of the world as appearance (the videhamukta leaves the world
  • hind). The two soteriologies diverge on the status of the world: the Pratyabhijñā liberates in the
  • rld (the jīvanmukta); Advaita liberates from the world (the appearance removed).

PART V — THE COMPARATIVE TABLE

  • Theme | Advaita Vedānta | IPVV (Pratyabhijñā) |
  • ------|----------------|---------------------|
  • Reality | nondual Brahman | one free Śiva |
  • Nature of consciousness | passive (witness) | free (svātantrya, agent) |
  • Plurality | illusory appearance | real manifestation (the self's reflection) |
  • Cause of plurality | anirvācyā avidyā (un-explainable ignorance) | svātantrya (the freedom to manifest) |
  • The world | superimposition (adhyāsa) | real reflection (pratibimba) |
  • The bondage | the ignorance-produced superimposition | the misreading of the real reflection as external |
  • Liberation | knowledge that removes the ignorance | recognition that re-cognizes the self |
  • The liberated | the jīva realizes it is Brahman (world left behind) | the jīvanmukta, free in the world (world recognized as self) |

PART VI — THE COMPARATIVE VERDICT

6.1 The IPVV's argumentative victory

  • the specific point of plurality, the IPVV has the argumentative advantage. The anti-anirvācya
  • gument (V3I) shows that the Advaitin's account of plurality is internally incoherent: the
  • -explainable ignorance cannot be located (not in Brahman, not in the souls), and the refutation
  • lf-undermines. The Pratyabhijñā's alternative — the difference is real, the self's own reflection — is
  • e only coherent account, because it locates the plurality in the freedom of consciousness rather than
  • a mysterious ignorance.

6.2 The two nondualisms, synthesized

  • t the comparison is not a simple victory. The two nondualisms agree on the deepest point — reality is
  • e nondual consciousness — and they diverge on the nature of that consciousness (passive vs. free),
  • e status of the world (illusory vs. real), and the cause of plurality (ignorance vs. freedom). The
  • vergence is systematic:
  • If consciousness is passive, the plurality needs an external cause (ignorance), and the world is
  • lusory.
  • If consciousness is free, the plurality comes from within (freedom), and the world is real.
  • The Pratyabhijñā's claim is that the passive reading is incoherent** (the anti-anirvācya argument)
  • d that the free reading alone makes sense of plurality, difference, action, and liberation (the whole
  • the IPVV). Advaita must posit an un-explainable ignorance to explain what the Pratyabhijñā explains
  • the freedom of consciousness. The IPVV's argument is that the ignorance is not an explanation but a
  • fusal to explain.

6.3 The one commitment

  • d the two nondualisms share the one commitment — the universalization. Both assert that reality is one
  • nsciousness. The felt→ground step — from the per-field consciousness to the one — is the commitment
  • th make. The IPVV argues it (the order-less support, V2O); Advaita asserts it (Brahman). Neither
  • rces it in the formal sense. The universalization is the nondual wager, shared by both despite their
  • vergence on everything else.

PART VII — THE SCHOLARLY CONCLUSION

  • e comparative synthesis of the IPVV and Advaita Vedānta yields five results:
  • The two nondualisms agree on the deepest point: reality is one nondual consciousness.
  • They diverge on the nature of consciousness: passive (Advaita) vs. free (Pratyabhijñā).
  • The IPVV's anti-anirvācya argument (V3I) shows the Advaitin's plurality is incoherent: the
  • -explainable ignorance cannot be located, and the refutation self-undermines.
  • The Pratyabhijñā's alternative is the pratibimbavāda: the difference is real, the self's own
  • flection; the bondage is the misreading of the real reflection as external.
  • Both share the one commitment: the universalization is the nondual wager.
